title: Bratz
full_review:
The sleazily dressed Bratz line of fashion dolls for preteen girls is somewhat akin to what "Grand Theft Auto" is for teenage boys: on the one hand, what some might consider "just" a game, on the other, a distinctly inappropriate pop-culture model.

The same can be said for the fluffy, live-action movie "Bratz" (Lionsgate), which envisions the dolls as four empowered Southern California high-schoolers who are good to their parents and classmates, do well in school and follow their dreams -- all the while, though, dressed like professional escorts or trashy music-video girls. The level of disconnect is quite mind-boggling.

Jewish-Hispanic Yasmin (Nathalia Ramos), Asian-Caucasian Jade (Janel Parrish), African-American Sasha (Logan Browning) and blonde Cloe (Skyler Shaye) are a multicultural quartet and friends since childhood. They wake each morning bright and happy, and immediately turn on their webcams to help each other pick outfits.

But on their first day as freshmen at Carry Nation High -- a rule-bound institution named for the temperance-movement icon who wielded a Bible and a hatchet -- three of them quickly hit the cliques: Brainy Jade sits with the science geeks, Sasha joins the cheerleading squad and Cloe makes the girls' soccer team. Yasmin doesn't fit in with those groups or any others, like the goths, the skateboarders, the theater kids or even the loners -- who in a lame attempt at humor have their own group.

Enforcing the system is student-body president Meredith Baxter Dimley (Chelsea Staub, who takes what could have been a one-note villain and makes her viciously manipulative yet vulnerable). The daughter of the school principal (Jon Voight, almost unrecognizable beneath a putty nose), Meredith dictates lunch-table seating, browbeats her minions and her boyfriend, and gathers embarrassing evidence with which to blackmail rivals.

When the movie jumps two years ahead to show our heroines having grown apart, Meredith throws herself an over-the-top party complete with MTV cameras and a trained elephant to upstage the four, whom she insults as "brats."

How her father, the public school principal, can bankroll a party that would bankrupt a pasha is left unexplained, but that conundrum is all in keeping with how director Sean McNamara swerves like a schizoid from naturalistic drama to such cartoon antics as Jade in chemistry class producing a fireworks display from a test tube.

Sitcom stereotypes -- from insult-machine younger siblings to a sassy student declaring "You did 'not' just say that!" -- abound. And for all the girls' good works and admirable camaraderie, the Bratz (as they name their singing-dancing girl group) are insufferable snobs.

In another example of the film's contradictory nature, the girls will all just "die" if they don't buy expensive new outfits for a party, and since struggling Cloe can't afford one, Sasha generously hands over one of her two prized gift certificates. "The Breakfast Club" similarly tackled high-school cliques, and looks like "Citizen Kane" by comparison.

The film contains much tight and skimpy costuming, two brawls and two instances of crude physical humor. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested. Some material may not be suitable for children.
